title: Ephemeral boost governor and proportional invoice adjustment playbook
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: design and implement an 'ephemeral boost governor' that provides short-term capacity boosts for Dedicated customers while ensuring transparent, proportional invoice adjustments and predictable unit economics. This ticket covers the policy, runtime guardrails, metering model, console/notification UX, operator runbook, and integration tests. Scope: dedicated fleets only; hosted API billing model is out-of-scope for this ticket. Objectives:

1) Policy semantics and enforcement: define a governor that grants time-limited boost tokens to tenants when autoscaling policies or surge pools are insufficient. Boosts should be preemptible, bounded by tenant-specific boost credit limits, and subject to global cluster safety caps. Policy includes: minimum grant duration, maximum continuous boost windows per 24h, cooldown windows, priority decay for repeated boosts, and emergency operator override.

2) Metering + invoice adjustments: implement proportional invoicing for boosts that distinguishes committed reserved capacity vs ephemeral usage. The accounting model must: (a) tag tokens with boost metadata (origin: surge-pool, governor, operator override), (b) compute per-tenant proportional adjustment factors to avoid surprise overage spikes on the invoice, (c) emit billing events with rounding rules and tie to existing billing pipeline. Design must include a clear formula for end-of-cycle crediting/charging and a short explanatory note for customers visible in Console billing breakdown.

3) Runtime implementation: add a BoostGovernor component in the fleet controller that: consults autoscaler state, current KV cache pressure, per-tenant soft quotas, and global safety headroom before granting boosts; exposes a REST admin API for operator actions; records durable boost allocations in control-plane state for reconciliation. Boosts must be isolated to avoid eviction cascades (i.e., do not cause disproportionate preemption of other tenants).

4) Observability: surface metrics (boost_grants_total, boost_duration_seconds_bucketed, boost_denials_total, boost_origin_labels, per-tenant boost_cost_estimate), distributed traces for boost lifecycle, and an alert if cluster-level boost consumption exceeds 65% of safety headroom.

5) UX & notifications: Console changes to show active boosts on tenant capacity page, historical boost timeline, and an automated email/Slack alert when a boost is granted or when a proportional invoice adjustment > 20% is expected. Provide a short modal that explains why a boost occurred and how charges will be reconciled.

6) Operator playbook: step-by-step actions for diagnosing excessive boosts (e.g., runaway model load, autoscaler misconfiguration, KV cache thrash), safe rollback, manual revoke, manual crediting adjustments, and PR/incident links.

7) Compatibility & rollout: toggle via runtime feature-flag per-cluster, gradual rollout in staging -> limited production fleets -> all Dedicated fleets. Backwards compatible: if control plane unrecognized the boost metadata, billing pipeline must treat ephemeral usage as regular overage with a placeholder tag; only when accounting is enabled will proportional adjustments apply.

Deliverables: design doc, controller implementation (Go), API schema (openapi snippet), Console UI mockups, billing pipeline adaptor, e2e tests and chaos test plan, operator runbook, customer-facing FAQ draft. Success criteria: 1) boosts reduce sustained p99 latency SLO violations for short spikes by 40% on pilot tenants without increasing median cost per token >5%, 2) no more than 2 customer-reported surprise invoice incidents during pilot, 3) automated tests and observability in place.

Risks and constraints: potential bill surprise if proportional adjustment is misunderstood; complexity in per-tenant metering at scale; eviction fairness when boost grants are frequent. Mitigations: conservative default limits, clear UI + billing notes, pilot with high-touch customers first, and operator rollback path.
comments: 2026-02-19 - Initial scoping discussion with PM. Agreed to scope to Dedicated only. PM requested billing transparency requirement and customer-facing messaging. Action: create design doc. - Aisha

2026-02-25 - Design doc v0 shared in Google Drive: https://drive.redwood.internal/d/boost-governor-v0. Feedback from Priya: clarify interaction with autoscaler (should never bypass hard caps) and require traceability for each boost. Action: add sequence diagrams and billing formula. - Jonah

2026-03-02 - Architecture review: decided to implement BoostGovernor as a control-plane module with persisted allocations to ensure reconciliation on controller restarts. Edge case: controller transient partitioning—added lease-based grant token with TTL and double-checked reconciliation logic. - Jonah

2026-03-05 - Billing meeting: agreed on proportional adjustment formula: prorated share = ephemeral_token_seconds * burst_unit_rate * (1 - committed_discount_factor). Need to validate with finance on rounding and minimum invoice line constraints. Action: open finance RFC. - Aisha

2026-03-08 - Implemented initial metrics and tracing hooks on the staging controller (branch: github.com/redwood/infra/boost-governor). Created PR #4782 for metrics and admin API. Early smoke tests show grants are limited correctly under synthetic spike. - Jonah

2026-03-10 - UX: Console mockups uploaded to Drive: https://drive.redwood.internal/d/boost-console-mockups. Product requested a small banner in billing page and an expandable explanation. Action: implement UI calls to billing events. - Priya

2026-03-12 - QA found an edge case where boost grants and autoscaler concurrent scaling lead to double-counting of requested GPUs in controller estimate. Added a reconciler change to compute a single in-flight allocation plan. Plan: hotfix patch today and re-run chaos test. - Jonah
